title: Backtracking & Bits
scopeHtml: Scope: backtracking template, permutations with duplicates, combination sum with pruning, N-Queens, bit manipulation.

notes.title: The backtracking template
notes.html:
Idea. Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time. After each choice you recurse; if the path fails (or finishes) you undo the choice and try the next. It explores a decision tree and prunes branches that cannot lead to a valid answer.

Recognise it when: "generate all subsets / permutations / combinations", "place N queens", "solve Sudoku", "find all paths", and input sizes are small (n ≤ 20).

The template.

  1. If the partial solution is complete, record it.
  2. For each available choice: choose it, recurse, un-choose it.
  3. Skip choices that violate constraints (pruning) and duplicates.

Worked example: Subsets (all subsets of distinct numbers). At each index either include the number or not; or equivalently loop over the next start positions.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void dfs(vector<int>& a, int start, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& out) {
    out.push_back(cur);                                   // every path is a valid subset
    for (int i = start; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        cur.push_back(a[i]);                              // choose
        dfs(a, i + 1, cur, out);                          // explore
        cur.pop_back();                                   // un-choose
    }
}
vector<vector<int>> subsets(vector<int>& a) {
    vector<vector<int>> out; vector<int> cur;
    dfs(a, 0, cur, out);
    return out;
}
void dfs(int[] a, int start, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
    out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur));                        // copy: cur keeps changing
    for (int i = start; i < a.length; i++) {
        cur.add(a[i]);                                    // choose
        dfs(a, i + 1, cur, out);                          // explore
        cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);                       // un-choose
    }
}
List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] a) {
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    dfs(a, 0, new ArrayList<>(), out);
    return out;
}
fun subsets(a: IntArray): List<List<Int>> {
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    val cur = mutableListOf<Int>()
    fun dfs(start: Int) {
        out.add(cur.toList())                             // copy: cur keeps changing
        for (i in start until a.size) {
            cur.add(a[i])                                 // choose
            dfs(i + 1)                                    // explore
            cur.removeAt(cur.size - 1)                    // un-choose
        }
    }
    dfs(0)
    return out
}
def subsets(a):
    out, cur = [], []

    def dfs(start):
        out.append(cur[:])                                # copy: cur keeps changing
        for i in range(start, len(a)):
            cur.append(a[i])                              # choose
            dfs(i + 1)                                    # explore
            cur.pop()                                     # un-choose

    dfs(0)
    return out

Complexity. There are 2^n subsets and copying each costs O(n), so O(n · 2^n) time; recursion depth O(n).

Industry examples. Constraint solvers, configuration generators, test-case combination generators, and puzzle solvers.

Everyday analogy. Exploring a maze: at every fork pick a path, and if it dead-ends walk back to the fork and try the next one.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding cur itself to the result instead of a copy; later mutations corrupt all results.
  • Forgetting to un-choose (the state leaks into other branches).
  • Using the loop-start index i + 1 versus start + 1 incorrectly, producing duplicates.

notes.title: Permutations and handling duplicates
notes.html:
Idea. For permutations, every unused element can be chosen at each position; track which are used. For inputs with duplicates, sort first and skip a value if it equals the previous one and the previous one is not currently in use, to avoid generating identical permutations.

Worked example: Permutations of distinct numbers.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void dfs(vector<int>& a, vector<bool>& used, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& out) {
    if (cur.size() == a.size()) { out.push_back(cur); return; }
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        if (used[i]) continue;
        used[i] = true; cur.push_back(a[i]);              // choose
        dfs(a, used, cur, out);
        cur.pop_back(); used[i] = false;                  // un-choose
    }
}
vector<vector<int>> permute(vector<int>& a) {
    vector<vector<int>> out; vector<int> cur; vector<bool> used(a.size(), false);
    dfs(a, used, cur, out);
    return out;
}
void dfs(int[] a, boolean[] used, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
    if (cur.size() == a.length) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur)); return; }
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (used[i]) continue;
        used[i] = true; cur.add(a[i]);                    // choose
        dfs(a, used, cur, out);
        cur.remove(cur.size() - 1); used[i] = false;      // un-choose
    }
}
List<List<Integer>> permute(int[] a) {
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    dfs(a, new boolean[a.length], new ArrayList<>(), out);
    return out;
}
fun permute(a: IntArray): List<List<Int>> {
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    val cur = mutableListOf<Int>()
    val used = BooleanArray(a.size)
    fun dfs() {
        if (cur.size == a.size) { out.add(cur.toList()); return }
        for (i in a.indices) {
            if (used[i]) continue
            used[i] = true; cur.add(a[i])                 // choose
            dfs()
            cur.removeAt(cur.size - 1); used[i] = false   // un-choose
        }
    }
    dfs()
    return out
}
def permute(a):
    out, cur, used = [], [], [False] * len(a)

    def dfs():
        if len(cur) == len(a):
            out.append(cur[:])
            return
        for i in range(len(a)):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            cur.append(a[i])                              # choose
            dfs()
            cur.pop()
            used[i] = False                               # un-choose

    dfs()
    return out

With duplicates. Sort the input; inside the loop add if i > 0 && a[i] == a[i-1] && !used[i-1] continue;.

Complexity. n! permutations, O(n · n!) time including copies.

Industry examples. Test-order generation, scheduling brute force on small instances, and cryptanalysis of small key spaces.

Everyday analogy. Seating guests at a table: try each unseated guest in the next seat, then reshuffle.

Common interview traps.

  • Duplicate results when the input has repeated values and sorting plus skipping is omitted.
  • Using used markers but forgetting to reset them.

notes.title: Combinations and pruning
notes.html:
Idea. Combination problems choose elements without regard to order, so recursion passes a start index to prevent reordering duplicates. Pruning cuts branches early, which turns hopeless exponential searches into feasible ones.

Worked example: Combination Sum (distinct candidates, each reusable unlimited times, find all unique combinations summing to target). Because reuse is allowed, recurse with the same index; sort and stop when a candidate exceeds the remaining target (pruning).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void dfs(vector<int>& c, int start, int remain, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& out) {
    if (remain == 0) { out.push_back(cur); return; }
    for (int i = start; i < (int)c.size() && c[i] <= remain; i++) {   // sorted: prune the rest
        cur.push_back(c[i]);
        dfs(c, i, remain - c[i], cur, out);                           // i, not i+1: reuse allowed
        cur.pop_back();
    }
}
vector<vector<int>> combinationSum(vector<int>& c, int target) {
    sort(c.begin(), c.end());
    vector<vector<int>> out; vector<int> cur;
    dfs(c, 0, target, cur, out);
    return out;
}
void dfs(int[] c, int start, int remain, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
    if (remain == 0) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur)); return; }
    for (int i = start; i < c.length && c[i] <= remain; i++) {        // sorted: prune the rest
        cur.add(c[i]);
        dfs(c, i, remain - c[i], cur, out);                           // i, not i+1: reuse allowed
        cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);
    }
}
List<List<Integer>> combinationSum(int[] c, int target) {
    Arrays.sort(c);
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    dfs(c, 0, target, new ArrayList<>(), out);
    return out;
}
fun combinationSum(input: IntArray, target: Int): List<List<Int>> {
    val c = input.sortedArray()
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    val cur = mutableListOf<Int>()
    fun dfs(start: Int, remain: Int) {
        if (remain == 0) { out.add(cur.toList()); return }
        var i = start
        while (i < c.size && c[i] <= remain) {                        // sorted: prune the rest
            cur.add(c[i])
            dfs(i, remain - c[i])                                     // i, not i+1: reuse allowed
            cur.removeAt(cur.size - 1)
            i++
        }
    }
    dfs(0, target)
    return out
}
def combination_sum(c, target):
    c.sort()
    out, cur = [], []

    def dfs(start, remain):
        if remain == 0:
            out.append(cur[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(c)):
            if c[i] > remain:
                break                                        # sorted: prune the rest
            cur.append(c[i])
            dfs(i, remain - c[i])                            # i, not i+1: reuse allowed
            cur.pop()

    dfs(0, target)
    return out

Complexity. Exponential in the worst case; pruning on the sorted candidates removes large parts of the tree.

Everyday analogy. Choosing coins to pay an exact price: once you have overshot, stop trying more coins on that path.

Common interview traps.

  • Using i + 1 when reuse is allowed (or i when it is not).
  • Producing the same combination in different orders (always iterate forward from start).
  • Forgetting to prune, leading to timeouts.

notes.title: N-Queens and constraint checks
notes.html:
Idea. Place queens row by row; maintain sets of used columns and diagonals so each placement check is O(1). Two cells share a diagonal when r - c is equal, and an anti-diagonal when r + c is equal.

Worked example: N-Queens (count the solutions).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int totalNQueens(int n) {
    vector<bool> col(n), d1(2 * n), d2(2 * n);                       // column, r-c+n, r+c
    function<int(int)> go = [&](int r) -> int {
        if (r == n) return 1;
        int count = 0;
        for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (col[c] || d1[r - c + n] || d2[r + c]) continue;      // attacked: prune
            col[c] = d1[r - c + n] = d2[r + c] = true;               // place
            count += go(r + 1);
            col[c] = d1[r - c + n] = d2[r + c] = false;              // remove
        }
        return count;
    };
    return go(0);
}
int totalNQueens(int n) { return go(0, n, new boolean[n], new boolean[2 * n], new boolean[2 * n]); }
int go(int r, int n, boolean[] col, boolean[] d1, boolean[] d2) {
    if (r == n) return 1;
    int count = 0;
    for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
        if (col[c] || d1[r - c + n] || d2[r + c]) continue;          // attacked: prune
        col[c] = d1[r - c + n] = d2[r + c] = true;                   // place
        count += go(r + 1, n, col, d1, d2);
        col[c] = d1[r - c + n] = d2[r + c] = false;                  // remove
    }
    return count;
}
fun totalNQueens(n: Int): Int {
    val col = BooleanArray(n)
    val d1 = BooleanArray(2 * n)
    val d2 = BooleanArray(2 * n)
    fun go(r: Int): Int {
        if (r == n) return 1
        var count = 0
        for (c in 0 until n) {
            if (col[c] || d1[r - c + n] || d2[r + c]) continue       // attacked: prune
            col[c] = true; d1[r - c + n] = true; d2[r + c] = true    // place
            count += go(r + 1)
            col[c] = false; d1[r - c + n] = false; d2[r + c] = false // remove
        }
        return count
    }
    return go(0)
}
def total_n_queens(n):
    col, d1, d2 = set(), set(), set()

    def go(r):
        if r == n:
            return 1
        count = 0
        for c in range(n):
            if c in col or (r - c) in d1 or (r + c) in d2:
                continue                                     # attacked: prune
            col.add(c); d1.add(r - c); d2.add(r + c)         # place
            count += go(r + 1)
            col.remove(c); d1.remove(r - c); d2.remove(r + c)  # remove
        return count

    return go(0)

Complexity. Roughly O(n!) in the worst case, but pruning cuts it dramatically (n = 8 has 92 solutions and only a few thousand explored nodes).

Industry examples. Sudoku and scheduling solvers, circuit layout and resource allocation with constraints (often via SAT or constraint-programming solvers).

Everyday analogy. Seating arrangements with rules such as "these two cannot sit together": reject a seat as soon as it breaks a rule.

Common interview traps.

  • Checking the entire board each time (O(n) check) instead of O(1) sets.
  • Forgetting to undo diagonal markers.
  • Wrong diagonal indexing (offset r - c by n to avoid negative indices).

notes.title: Bit manipulation essentials
notes.html:
Idea. Numbers are bit patterns; bitwise operations are O(1) and can replace sets, flags and loops.

Core operations.

  • x & 1 odd check; x >> 1 divide by two; x << 1 multiply by two.
  • x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit (count bits, power-of-two check: x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0).
  • x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x: XOR cancels pairs.
  • 1 << i sets up a mask for bit i; a bitmask can represent a subset of up to ~20-30 items.

Worked example: Single Number (every element appears twice except one; find it in O(n) time, O(1) space). XOR everything: pairs cancel.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int singleNumber(vector<int>& a) {
    int x = 0;
    for (int v : a) x ^= v;                               // pairs cancel
    return x;
}
int countBits(unsigned int x) {
    int c = 0;
    while (x) { x &= x - 1; c++; }                        // clears the lowest set bit
    return c;
}
int singleNumber(int[] a) {
    int x = 0;
    for (int v : a) x ^= v;                               // pairs cancel
    return x;
}
int countBits(int x) {
    int c = 0;
    while (x != 0) { x &= x - 1; c++; }                   // clears the lowest set bit
    return c;                                             // or Integer.bitCount(x)
}
fun singleNumber(a: IntArray): Int = a.fold(0) { acc, v -> acc xor v }   // pairs cancel

fun countBits(x0: Int): Int {
    var x = x0
    var c = 0
    while (x != 0) { x = x and (x - 1); c++ }             // clears the lowest set bit
    return c                                              // or x0.countOneBits()
}
def single_number(a):
    x = 0
    for v in a:
        x ^= v                                            # pairs cancel
    return x

def count_bits(x):
    c = 0
    while x:
        x &= x - 1                                        # clears the lowest set bit
        c += 1
    return c                                              # or bin(x).count("1") / x.bit_count()

Bitmask subsets. Enumerate all subsets of n items with for mask in 0 .. (1<<n)-1 and test bit i with (mask >> i) & 1; used in small DP (travelling salesman) and subset problems.

Language gotchas for a C++ developer. Java and Kotlin int are 32-bit signed and >> is an arithmetic shift (use >>> in Java, ushr in Kotlin for a logical shift); C++ right shift of negatives is implementation-defined before C++20; Python integers are unbounded, so use masks like & 0xFFFFFFFF to emulate 32 bits.

Industry examples. Permission flags, feature-flag sets, bitmap indexes in databases, Bloom filters, compact state in game engines and network protocols.

Everyday analogy. A row of light switches: each switch is one bit, and flipping many at once is a single operation.

Common interview traps.

  • Operator precedence: x & 1 == 0 parses as x & (1 == 0); parenthesise.
  • Shifting by 32 or more is undefined/incorrect for 32-bit types.
  • Sign extension on negative numbers with arithmetic shifts.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Backtracking is choose, explore, un-choose over a decision tree; copy the current path when recording results, use a start index for combinations (same index when reuse is allowed), a used array for permutations, and sort plus skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicates. Prune with early checks (sorted candidates, O(1) column and diagonal sets in N-Queens) to make it feasible. Bit tricks such as x & (x - 1), XOR cancelling and bitmask subsets give compact O(1) operations; mind operator precedence, signed shifts and 32-bit limits.

questions.promptHtml: Generate all subsets of an array. Explain choose, explore and un-choose, and the most common bug.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The foundation for all backtracking problems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Record the current path as a subset, then for each index from start choose the element, recurse with i + 1, and un-choose it by removing the element. The most common bug is adding the live list itself to the results instead of a copy, so later mutations corrupt every stored answer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
There are 2^n subsets and copying each costs O(n), so total time is O(n · 2^n). The recursion depth is n. Forgetting to undo the choice leaks state into sibling branches.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void dfs(vector<int>& a, int start, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& out) {
    out.push_back(cur);
    for (int i = start; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        cur.push_back(a[i]);
        dfs(a, i + 1, cur, out);
        cur.pop_back();
    }
}
void dfs(int[] a, int start, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
    out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur));
    for (int i = start; i < a.length; i++) {
        cur.add(a[i]);
        dfs(a, i + 1, cur, out);
        cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);
    }
}
fun subsets(a: IntArray): List<List<Int>> {
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    val cur = mutableListOf<Int>()
    fun dfs(start: Int) {
        out.add(cur.toList())
        for (i in start until a.size) {
            cur.add(a[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            cur.removeAt(cur.size - 1)
        }
    }
    dfs(0)
    return out
}
def subsets(a):
    out, cur = [], []

    def dfs(start):
        out.append(cur[:])
        for i in range(start, len(a)):
            cur.append(a[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            cur.pop()

    dfs(0)
    return out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing the reference to cur instead of a copy.
  • Forgetting to un-choose.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Subsets with duplicates? → Sort and skip equal neighbours at the same recursion level.
  2. Iterative alternative? → Bitmask enumeration of 0 to 2^n - 1.
  3. Complexity? → O(n · 2^n).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions both the recursion tree and the bitmask method.

questions.promptHtml: Generate all permutations. How do you avoid duplicate permutations when the input contains repeated values?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Duplicate handling is the usual follow-up.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Track which indices are used; at each position try every unused element, recurse, then restore. For repeated values, sort the input and skip an element if it equals the previous one and the previous one is not currently used, so identical values are placed in a fixed order. n! results, O(n · n!) time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without the skip rule, equal values at different indices generate the same permutation multiple times. The !used[i-1] condition ensures the earlier duplicate is placed first within a given prefix.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void dfs(vector<int>& a, vector<bool>& used, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& out) {
    if (cur.size() == a.size()) { out.push_back(cur); return; }
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        if (used[i]) continue;
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]) continue;     // duplicate skip (sorted input)
        used[i] = true; cur.push_back(a[i]);
        dfs(a, used, cur, out);
        cur.pop_back(); used[i] = false;
    }
}
void dfs(int[] a, boolean[] used, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
    if (cur.size() == a.length) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur)); return; }
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (used[i]) continue;
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]) continue;     // duplicate skip (sorted input)
        used[i] = true; cur.add(a[i]);
        dfs(a, used, cur, out);
        cur.remove(cur.size() - 1); used[i] = false;
    }
}
fun permuteUnique(input: IntArray): List<List<Int>> {
    val a = input.sortedArray()
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    val cur = mutableListOf<Int>()
    val used = BooleanArray(a.size)
    fun dfs() {
        if (cur.size == a.size) { out.add(cur.toList()); return }
        for (i in a.indices) {
            if (used[i]) continue
            if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]) continue   // duplicate skip
            used[i] = true; cur.add(a[i])
            dfs()
            cur.removeAt(cur.size - 1); used[i] = false
        }
    }
    dfs()
    return out
}
def permute_unique(a):
    a.sort()
    out, cur, used = [], [], [False] * len(a)

    def dfs():
        if len(cur) == len(a):
            out.append(cur[:])
            return
        for i in range(len(a)):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]:
                continue                                      # duplicate skip
            used[i] = True
            cur.append(a[i])
            dfs()
            cur.pop()
            used[i] = False

    dfs()
    return out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Skipping the sort step.
  • Not resetting used.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. k-th permutation without generating all? → Factorial number system.
  2. Next permutation in place? → Find the pivot, swap with the next larger, reverse the suffix.
  3. Complexity of unique permutations? → Bounded by n!/(product of duplicate counts!).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains the duplicate rule and the next-permutation algorithm.

questions.promptHtml: Solve Combination Sum where candidates can be reused. How do you avoid duplicate combinations and prune the search?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests index discipline and pruning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Sort the candidates, then recurse with a start index. Because a number can be reused, recurse with the same index i; iterate forward only so each combination appears once. Stop the loop when a candidate exceeds the remaining target, which prunes all larger candidates.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Using i + 1 would forbid reuse; going back to index 0 each time would generate permutations of the same combination. Sorting makes the break pruning valid. Exponential in the worst case but practical with pruning.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void dfs(vector<int>& c, int start, int remain, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& out) {
    if (remain == 0) { out.push_back(cur); return; }
    for (int i = start; i < (int)c.size() && c[i] <= remain; i++) {
        cur.push_back(c[i]);
        dfs(c, i, remain - c[i], cur, out);
        cur.pop_back();
    }
}
void dfs(int[] c, int start, int remain, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
    if (remain == 0) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur)); return; }
    for (int i = start; i < c.length && c[i] <= remain; i++) {
        cur.add(c[i]);
        dfs(c, i, remain - c[i], cur, out);
        cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);
    }
}
fun combinationSum(input: IntArray, target: Int): List<List<Int>> {
    val c = input.sortedArray()
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    val cur = mutableListOf<Int>()
    fun dfs(start: Int, remain: Int) {
        if (remain == 0) { out.add(cur.toList()); return }
        var i = start
        while (i < c.size && c[i] <= remain) {
            cur.add(c[i])
            dfs(i, remain - c[i])
            cur.removeAt(cur.size - 1)
            i++
        }
    }
    dfs(0, target)
    return out
}
def combination_sum(c, target):
    c.sort()
    out, cur = [], []

    def dfs(start, remain):
        if remain == 0:
            out.append(cur[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(c)):
            if c[i] > remain:
                break
            cur.append(c[i])
            dfs(i, remain - c[i])
            cur.pop()

    dfs(0, target)
    return out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• i + 1 when reuse is allowed.
  • Restarting from index 0 and generating permutations.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Each number used once with duplicates in input? → Sort, use i + 1, skip equal neighbours.
  2. Only count the combinations? → DP (like coin change) is much faster.
  3. When does backtracking blow up? → Large targets with small candidates; switch to DP for counts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior switches to DP when only the count is needed.

questions.promptHtml: Count the ways to place N queens on an N×N board. How do you make the attack check O(1)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic constraint-backtracking problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Place one queen per row and keep three boolean sets: used columns, used diagonals identified by r - c, and used anti-diagonals identified by r + c. A square is safe if none of its three keys is used, making the check O(1). Place, recurse to the next row, then remove. The search is pruned heavily, far below n!.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rows are handled by recursion (exactly one queen per row), so only columns and diagonals need tracking. Offset r - c by n for array indexing. For a bitmask version, use three integers and bit tricks to enumerate free columns quickly.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int totalNQueens(int n) {
    vector<bool> col(n), d1(2 * n), d2(2 * n);
    function<int(int)> go = [&](int r) -> int {
        if (r == n) return 1;
        int count = 0;
        for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (col[c] || d1[r - c + n] || d2[r + c]) continue;
            col[c] = d1[r - c + n] = d2[r + c] = true;
            count += go(r + 1);
            col[c] = d1[r - c + n] = d2[r + c] = false;
        }
        return count;
    };
    return go(0);
}
int totalNQueens(int n) { return go(0, n, new boolean[n], new boolean[2 * n], new boolean[2 * n]); }
int go(int r, int n, boolean[] col, boolean[] d1, boolean[] d2) {
    if (r == n) return 1;
    int count = 0;
    for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
        if (col[c] || d1[r - c + n] || d2[r + c]) continue;
        col[c] = d1[r - c + n] = d2[r + c] = true;
        count += go(r + 1, n, col, d1, d2);
        col[c] = d1[r - c + n] = d2[r + c] = false;
    }
    return count;
}
fun totalNQueens(n: Int): Int {
    val col = BooleanArray(n)
    val d1 = BooleanArray(2 * n)
    val d2 = BooleanArray(2 * n)
    fun go(r: Int): Int {
        if (r == n) return 1
        var count = 0
        for (c in 0 until n) {
            if (col[c] || d1[r - c + n] || d2[r + c]) continue
            col[c] = true; d1[r - c + n] = true; d2[r + c] = true
            count += go(r + 1)
            col[c] = false; d1[r - c + n] = false; d2[r + c] = false
        }
        return count
    }
    return go(0)
}
def total_n_queens(n):
    col, d1, d2 = set(), set(), set()

    def go(r):
        if r == n:
            return 1
        count = 0
        for c in range(n):
            if c in col or (r - c) in d1 or (r + c) in d2:
                continue
            col.add(c); d1.add(r - c); d2.add(r + c)
            count += go(r + 1)
            col.remove(c); d1.remove(r - c); d2.remove(r + c)
        return count

    return go(0)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Scanning the whole board for conflicts.
  • Wrong diagonal index or forgetting to undo markers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Return the boards? → Record column per row and build strings at the leaves.
  2. Speed up? → Bitmask version and symmetry (mirror) halving.
  3. Sudoku solver? → Same pattern with row, column and box sets plus "most constrained cell first" heuristic.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior adds bitmask optimisation and the heuristic ordering for Sudoku.

questions.promptHtml: Find the number that appears once in an array where every other number appears twice, in O(n) time and O(1) space. Then count the set bits of a number.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests bitwise reasoning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: XOR all numbers: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so pairs cancel and the single value remains. To count set bits, repeat x &= x - 1, which clears the lowest set bit, and count iterations. Both are O(n) and O(1) space respectively, and x & (x - 1) == 0 tests for a power of two.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and all bits below it, so AND-ing with the original clears exactly that bit. Language helpers: __builtin_popcount (C++), Integer.bitCount (Java), countOneBits() (Kotlin), int.bit_count() (Python 3.10+).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int singleNumber(vector<int>& a) {
    int x = 0;
    for (int v : a) x ^= v;
    return x;
}
int countBits(unsigned int x) {
    int c = 0;
    while (x) { x &= x - 1; c++; }
    return c;
}
int singleNumber(int[] a) {
    int x = 0;
    for (int v : a) x ^= v;
    return x;
}
int countBits(int x) {
    int c = 0;
    while (x != 0) { x &= x - 1; c++; }
    return c;
}
fun singleNumber(a: IntArray): Int = a.fold(0) { acc, v -> acc xor v }

fun countBits(x0: Int): Int {
    var x = x0
    var c = 0
    while (x != 0) { x = x and (x - 1); c++ }
    return c
}
def single_number(a):
    x = 0
    for v in a:
        x ^= v
    return x

def count_bits(x):
    c = 0
    while x:
        x &= x - 1
        c += 1
    return c

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Operator precedence: x & 1 == 0 needs parentheses.
  • Arithmetic versus logical right shift on negatives in Java/Kotlin (>>> / ushr).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Every number appears three times except one? → Count bits mod 3 per position, or use two accumulators.
  2. Two numbers appear once? → XOR all, split by a differing bit, XOR each group.
  3. Enumerate all subsets with bits? → Loop masks 0 to (1 << n) - 1.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior handles the two-singles and three-times variants and knows language gotchas.

questions.contextHtml: A configuration validator for an infrastructure tool tries every combination of 28 optional feature flags to check for conflicts. It worked with 15 flags in seconds, but with 28 flags the job runs for days and exhausts memory because it stores every combination before checking.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, and how would you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Runs it on a bigger machine or in parallel on more machines.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are conflicts pairwise or involve larger groups? Do we need all valid combinations or just a yes/no? How often do flags change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop storing combinations; stream-check them and cap the run time.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 2^28 ≈ 268 million combinations (about 2^13 = 8,000 times more than with 15 flags); storing them all uses O(2^n) memory; the checks are repeated redundantly.
  4. How I'd verify: Compute the count, measure time per check and memory per stored combination.
  5. Root cause: Exponential growth with no pruning and no streaming.
  6. Fix: Use backtracking with pruning: add a flag only if it does not conflict with already-chosen flags and abandon the branch immediately on conflict. If conflicts are pairwise, the problem reduces to a graph (conflict graph), and "valid sets" are independent sets, so many properties can be checked on the graph in polynomial time without enumeration. Or encode the rules as a SAT/constraint solver problem and ask the solver whether a conflicting combination exists.
  7. Prevention: Test with the maximum realistic input size, add complexity warnings, and avoid materialising exponential result sets.
  8. Trade-offs: Solvers add a dependency but scale far better; pairwise checks are simple and fast; enumerating is only acceptable for small n.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need to list every valid combination? → Stream them lazily with a generator and set a limit.
  • Flags have dependencies (A requires B)? → Add implication constraints to the solver or prune in the recursion.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Replacing a brute-force combination scan with pairwise conflict checks and a SAT solver turned a multi-day job into milliseconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more hardware.
  • Hire: spots exponential growth and adds pruning/streaming.
  • Strong hire: reformulates as a graph or SAT problem and handles the "list everything" case lazily.
